slides.title: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
slides.subtitle: From a sip of ORS to a boat on the river — the science of mixing things together, and of what floats and what sinks.
points: What happens when you add too much sugar to your tea and it stops dissolving — how can you fix it?
Why do sugar and salt dissolve in water but not in oil, and why is water called a good solvent?
Why are water bottles usually tall and cylindrical instead of spherical?

slides.title: Why every sip of ORS tastes the same
slides.body: Every sip of an **Oral Rehydration Solution (ORS)** tastes the same — never salty in one and sweet in another — because the salt and sugar spread **evenly throughout** the water. That is a **uniform mixture**. But **chalk powder, sand, or sawdust** in water stay **unevenly spread** — a **non-uniform mixture**.

slides.title: What are solute, solvent, and solution?
slides.intro: A uniform mixture like salt in water has a special name — and so do its parts. Let's name them.

slides.title: Solute + Solvent → Solution
slides.body: A uniform mixture, like salt or sugar in water, is a **solution**. When a solid mixes into a liquid, the solid that dissolves is the **solute** and the liquid it dissolves in is the **solvent**. The solute spreads **evenly all through** the solvent.

slides.title: Smaller amount is the solute
slides.body: When two **liquids** mix, it isn't always clear which dissolves which. The rule: the substance in the **smaller amount** is the **solute**, and the one in the **larger amount** is the **solvent**.

slides.title: The chashni of gulab jamun
slides.body: The **chashni** (sugar syrup) of gulab jamun is a **large amount of sugar** (solid) dissolved in a **small amount of water** (liquid). Yet the water is still counted as the **solvent** and the sugar as the **solute** — the solid-in-liquid rule wins.

slides.title: How much solute can a fixed amount of solvent dissolve?
slides.intro: Keep adding salt to a glass of water — does it dissolve forever, or is there a limit?

slides.title: How much salt will water take?
slides.purpose: We want to find out whether water can dissolve salt **without limit**. So we keep adding salt, spoon by spoon, and watch for the moment it stops disappearing.
steps: Fill — half-fill a clean glass tumbler with water
Dissolve — add one spoon of salt and stir until it vanishes completely
Keep going — add salt spoon by spoon, recording each in Table 9.1, until it stops dissolving and settles
slides.observe: At first the salt **dissolves fully**. After a few more spoons, the added salt **no longer dissolves** and settles at the bottom — the water has **reached its limit** and can take no more salt at that temperature.

slides.title: Saturated or unsaturated?
slides.leftBody: More solute can **still dissolve** in it at that temperature.
slides.rightBody: The water has **reached its limit** — extra salt just settles, undissolved, at the bottom.

slides.title: Concentration and solubility
slides.body: **Concentration** is how much solute sits in a fixed amount of solution — **dilute** (less, like one spoon) or **concentrated** (more, like two or more); these are **relative** terms. The **maximum** solute that dissolves in a fixed quantity of solvent at a given temperature is its **solubility** — beyond it, the rest stays undissolved.

slides.title: How does temperature affect solubility?
slides.intro: A saturated solution won't take more solute — unless we warm it. Let's test that.

slides.title: Warm the water, dissolve more
slides.purpose: We want to see whether **heat changes how much** a solid can dissolve. So we saturate water with baking soda, then heat it and watch the leftover solid.
steps: Measure — take about 50 mL of water at 20 °C and add baking soda, stirring, until some stays undissolved
Heat — warm the contents to 50 °C while stirring, then add more baking soda until some remains undissolved again
Heat further — raise it to 70 °C while stirring and watch the leftover solid
slides.observe: Each time you **heat the water, the undissolved baking soda dissolves** — and you can add even more. For **most solids, solubility increases with temperature**, so a saturated solution behaves as an **unsaturated** one when warmed.

slides.translation: Asima Chatterjee used solvents and solutions extensively to extract and isolate important compounds from medicinal plants. She was the second Indian woman to earn a Doctorate of Science, the first woman to win the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Award in chemical science, and was honoured with the Padma Bhushan.

slides.title: Solubility of gases
slides.intro: Solids dissolve in water — but what about gases? And does the temperature rule still hold?

slides.title: The oxygen that keeps fish alive
slides.body: Many gases, including **oxygen**, dissolve evenly in water — only a **small amount**, but enough that this dissolved oxygen **sustains plants, fishes, and aquatic organisms**. Unlike solids, gas solubility **decreases as temperature rises**: **cold water holds more oxygen**, and warming water drives it out — the opposite of how solids behave.

slides.title: Why do objects float or sink in water?
slides.intro: Husk floats while rice sinks; oil floats while a stone drops. What decides it?

slides.title: Lighter floats, heavier sinks
slides.body: Some objects **float** and others **sink** — husk floats while rice sinks; oil floats on water. Generally, floaters are **lighter** than the liquid and sinkers are **heavier**. A wooden stick and an iron rod of the **same size** feel different — that property is **density**. Note: density is **not the only factor** deciding what floats in a given liquid.

slides.title: What is density?
slides.intro: A crowded bus, a dense forest — density is about how much is packed into a space. Let's define it.

slides.title: Mass packed into a unit volume
slides.body: Imagine a **crowded bus** versus one with few people — that is high versus low density. **Density** is the **mass in a unit volume** of a substance: **Density = Mass ÷ Volume**, independent of shape or size. Its **SI unit is kg/m³**, but for liquids and solids we use **g/cm³**. An aluminium block of **27 g** and **10 cm³** is **2.7 g/cm³** — **2.7 times denser than water** (its relative density).

slides.title: Determination of density
slides.intro: Density = Mass ÷ Volume — so first we measure mass, then volume. Let's do both.

slides.title: Weigh a stone on a balance
slides.purpose: To find density we first need the object's **mass**. So we use a **digital weighing balance**, taring it so the watch glass doesn't count.
steps: Zero — switch on the balance and press tare or reset so it reads zero
Tare — place a dry watch glass on the pan and tare it back to zero
Weigh — set the stone on the watch glass and note the mass, say 16.400 g
slides.observe: The balance reads the **mass of the stone alone**, because taring cancelled the watch glass. **Mass** is the quantity of matter in an object — and most balances actually sense weight but show it in **mass units** (g or kg).

slides.title: Find a stone's volume by displacement
slides.purpose: A stone has an **irregular shape**, so we can't use length × width × height. Instead we measure how much **water it pushes aside** in a measuring cylinder.
steps: Fill — pour water into a measuring cylinder to a known mark, say 50 mL, and record it
Lower — tie the stone with a thread and gently lower it in until fully submerged
Subtract — read the new level, say 55 mL; the volume of water displaced (55 − 50 = 5 mL) is the stone's volume, 5 cm³
slides.observe: The water **rises by exactly the volume of the stone** — the displaced water (in mL) equals the stone's volume (in **cm³** for solids). Read the level at the **bottom of the meniscus**, with your eyes at its level.

slides.title: From mass and volume to density
slides.body: With both numbers in hand, we just divide. For our stone: **Density = Mass ÷ Volume = 16.400 g ÷ 5 cm³ = 3.28 g/cm³**. Since that is greater than water's **1 g/cm³**, this stone would **sink**.

slides.title: Lighter than water floats
slides.caption: Change the object's density. Below water's 1.0 g/cm³ it floats (and rides lower as it gets denser); above 1.0 it sinks.

slides.title: Effect of temperature on density
slides.intro: Heat something and it spreads out — what does that do to its density?

slides.title: Why hot air rises
slides.body: On heating, particles **move apart and spread**, so **volume grows while mass stays the same** — and since density = mass ÷ volume, the **density decreases**. Hot air is **less dense** than the cool air around it, so it rises — exactly how a **hot air balloon** lifts off.

slides.title: Bamboo rafts and Earth's dense core
slides.body: Before big ships, people tied **bamboo poles** into rafts — bamboo is light, hollow, and floats easily. Deep inside our planet, **pressure and temperature rise**, packing materials tighter — so the Earth's layers get **denser from the crust down to the core**.

slides.title: Effect of pressure on density
slides.intro: Squeeze a gas and it shrinks — but does pressure change liquids and solids the same way?

slides.title: Pressure mostly affects gases
slides.body: For **gases**, more pressure pushes particles closer, so volume **drops** and density **rises**. **Liquids** are nearly incompressible, so pressure has only a **small effect**, and **solids** are affected even less — their density change under pressure is **usually negligible**.

slides.title: Why ice floats on water
slides.body: Water is densest at **4 °C**. As it cools to **0 °C** and freezes, its particles arrange to take up **more space** — an **expansion**. The same water now fills a larger volume, so its density **drops** and ice **floats**. That floating ice layer keeps the water below warm enough for fish to survive.
